Brushy areas are abundant with dwarf [manzanita](/wiki/Manzanita "Manzanita") and ceanothus; the unique [Sierra puffball](/wiki/Calvatia_sculpta "Calvatia sculpta") is also found here. Right below the timberline, in the Hudsonian zone, the whitebark, foxtail, and silver pines grow. At about 10,500 feet (3,200 m), begins the Arctic zone, a treeless region whose flora include a number of wildflowers, including [Sierra primrose](/wiki/Primula_suffrutescens "Primula suffrutescens"), [yellow columbine](/wiki/Aquilegia_flavescens "Aquilegia flavescens"), [alpine buttercup](/wiki/Ranunculus "Ranunculus"), and [alpine shooting star](/wiki/Dodecatheon_alpinum "Dodecatheon alpinum").[[155]](#cite_note-California:_flora_and_fauna-157)[[157]](#cite_note-Life_Zones_of_the_Central_Sierra_Nevada-159)

Continent :: Etymology :: chunk_0001
From the 16th century the English noun *continent* was derived from the term *continent land*, meaning continuous or connected land[[5]](#cite_note-oed-5) and translated from the Latin *terra continens*.[[6]](#cite_note-6) The noun was used to mean "a connected or continuous tract of land" or [mainland](/wiki/Mainland "Mainland").[[5]](#cite_note-oed-5) It was not applied only to very large areas of land—in the 17th century, references were made to the *continents* (or mainlands) of the [Isle of Man](/wiki/Isle_of_Man "Isle of Man"), [Ireland](/wiki/Ireland "Ireland") and [Wales](/wiki/Wales "Wales") and in 1745 to [Sumatra](/wiki/Sumatra "Sumatra").[[5]](#cite_note-oed-5) The word *continent* was used in translating Greek and Latin writings about the three "parts" of the world, although in the original languages no word of exactly the same meaning as *continent* was used.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewis_&_Wigen,_The_Myth_of_Continents199729-7)

While *continent* was used on the one hand for relatively small areas of continuous land, on the other hand geographers again raised Herodotus's query about why a single large landmass should be divided into separate continents. In the mid-17th century, [Peter Heylin](/wiki/Peter_Heylin "Peter Heylin") wrote in his *Cosmographie* that "A Continent is a great quantity of Land, not separated by any Sea from the rest of the World, as the whole Continent of Europe, Asia, Africa." In 1727, [Ephraim Chambers](/wiki/Ephraim_Chambers "Ephraim Chambers") wrote in his *Cyclopædia,* "The world is ordinarily divided into two grand continents: the [Old](/wiki/Old_World "Old World") and the [New](/wiki/New_World "New World")." And in his 1752 atlas, [Emanuel Bowen](/wiki/Emanuel_Bowen "Emanuel Bowen") defined a continent as "a large space of dry land comprehending many countries all joined together, without any separation by water. Thus Europe, Asia, and Africa is one great continent, as America is another."[[8]](#cite_note-8) However, the old idea of Europe, Asia and Africa as "parts" of the world ultimately persisted with these being regarded as separate continents.

McDonough was born on December 2, 1969, in [Stillwater, Minnesota](/wiki/Stillwater,_Minnesota "Stillwater, Minnesota").[[3]](#cite_note-nytimes_20081123-3) He was one of 11 children in a devout [Irish Catholic](/wiki/Irish_Catholics "Irish Catholics") family, his grandparents having [emigrated](/wiki/Emigration "Emigration") from [Connemara](/wiki/Connemara "Connemara") in the [Gaeltacht](/wiki/Gaeltacht "Gaeltacht").[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-O'Dowd-2013-5)

According to some accounts, Quaker Mill partner Henry Seymour came up with the brand name after discovering an encyclopedia article about [Quakers](/wiki/Quakers "Quakers"). > On each side of said flag in the center thereof, must be embroidered or stamped an eagle with outspread wings and with opened beak. The eagle must be three feet four inches [101.6 centimeters] from tip to tip of wing, and one foot ten inches [55.88 centimeters] from top of head to bottom of olive branch hereinafter described. The left foot of the eagle shall grasp a sheaf of arrows, the right foot shall grasp an olive branch showing three red berries. On the breast of the eagle must be displayed a shield, the lower part showing seven red and six white stripes placed alternately. Through the open beak of the eagle must pass a scroll bearing the words 'E Pluribus Unum'. Beneath the eagle there must be a scroll on which must be borne the words 'North Dakota'.
